title: Twenty-two claimants at Bakala
hookLine: tradition says the trader Makhan Shah found the true Guru meditating in Bakala among many false claimants
tomorrow: journeys east and a new town

lines: EVERYONE CLAIMS TO BE THE REAL ONE.
cards: Search for almost anything online and a dozen people shout that they're the real one. The original recipe. The authentic brand.
The only true expert. The loudest voice gets the top of the page. Now go to Bakala in 1664, after the child Guru's last words, Baba Bakale, reached Punjab.
The next Guru is at Bakala. So, overnight, Bakala fills up with Gurus. Relatives of the Guru's family set up seats, gather followers, and announce themselves.
Tradition says there were twenty-two of them. Somewhere in the village, a quiet man sits in a room below ground, saying nothing.

teach.h: A VOW IN A STORM AT SEA.
teach.b: The story Sikhs tell turns on Makhan Shah, a trader who shipped goods by sea.
Tradition says his ship was caught in a terrible storm, and in his fear he vowed: if I reach land safely, I'll give five hundred gold coins to the Guru. The ship survived.
He came to Punjab to keep his promise, and arrived in Bakala to find twenty-two Gurus. How do you choose? He had a quiet plan.
He went to each claimant in turn, bowed, and laid down just two gold coins. Each one accepted the coins, blessed him, and thanked him. None of them knew about the vow.
Then someone told him there was one more: a man who lived simply, meditating in a small room, and made no claim at all. Makhan Shah found Tegh Bahadur, bowed, and laid down two coins.
Tradition says the quiet man looked up and said, gently: you promised five hundred. The merchant knew.
He ran up onto the roof and shouted over the whole village, again and again: I've found the Guru!
I've found the Guru! And so the man who had been brave, then quiet, became the ninth Guru. The real one wasn't the loudest.

He wasn't even competing. He didn't tell Makhan Shah he was the Guru; he simply knew the truth of the man's heart. And the one who recognized him was not a scholar or a priest, but a trader who had kept his word.

how: Sikhs retell the story of Makhan Shah finding Guru Tegh Bahadur at Bakala, and his cry 'Guru ladho re', the Guru is found, is remembered at the gurdwara in Baba Bakala.

o: one of the twenty-two who claimed to be Guru
a Mughal tax collector stationed at Bakala
the trader who kept his vow and found the Guru

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a trader saved from a storm
what he laid before each claimant
where he shouted the Guru is found

he made no claim. he simply named the vow no one else knew.
the claimants each accepted two coins and blessed him
none of them knew about the five hundred.
the Guru was recognized by a group of scholars

games.q: you're Makhan Shah. you vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru, and you've found twenty-two Gurus. what do you do?
o: give five hundred to the one with the most followers.
lay two coins before each, and wait.
split the five hundred between them all.
games.why: he laid two coins before each claimant. only the quiet man in the room below said: you promised five hundred.

practice: Think of a question in your life where lots of voices are competing: a decision, a worry, a piece of news. Notice the loudest one and set it aside for a moment.
Then listen for a quieter voice you've been walking past: a friend who said little, a feeling you haven't heard out, your own sense of what's true.

wordCard.voice: Makhan Shah. The merchant who tested twenty-two claimants at Bakala with two gold coins each, and found the true Guru, Tegh Bahadur, meditating quietly.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the Guru is found, Makhan Shah's cry from the rooftop.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru is found. Twenty-two seats, and the true one made no claim. See you tomorrow.
